input.reason: Quest predicted ≥0.70 fresh unassisted accuracy on inverted multiplicative reasoning; Lab Learner returned 3/3 unseen, unassisted, unconfounded correct readings (accuracy 1.00), and the predicted 'factor-pair overgeneralization' error never appeared. That supports the transfer hypothesis at the level Quest can support it — inversion on unseen number families held. But the Quest responses that were logged ('6 groups of 4 = 24', '7', '5 × 6 = 30') are single-step recoveries, and nothing in the record shows him rejecting a total that admits no equal split, nor coordinating two unknowns under conflicting constraints. Boss eligibility is met with fresh correct unassisted Quest evidence, so the honest next move is unseen synthesis: force him to choose which quantity is unknown, defend a claim that a division is impossible, and pay a real cost when he forces a split that does not exist.
input.nextAcademicTarget: Synthesis of multiplicative inversion: from a known total, recover an unknown group count or an unknown group size when the word problem does not say which is missing, and identify totals that cannot be split equally into a demanded number of equal groups — justifying the impossibility rather than rounding, dropping, or forcing a remainder.
input.nextMechanic: A loading-dock crate press where the child drags crates into a fixed number of shipping bays or sets the bay count itself, and must slam a red REFUSE lever on any order whose total cannot fill every bay evenly.
input.nextTheme: Night shift at a river cargo dock. Orders come down a conveyor from a impatient dispatcher. Every barge leaves whether Lab Learner is ready or not.
input.nextOpeningPurpose: Open on a conveyor already moving with one order on it and the REFUSE lever glowing, so the very first thing the child learns is that some orders are supposed to be thrown back — before any correct answer trains him to always find a split.
input.nextCreatorPrompt: Build a night-shift cargo dock for a 9-year-old who has already proven he can find a missing factor on unseen numbers. Six orders ride a conveyor toward the barge. Each order is a short dispatcher line, never labeled with what is unknown: sometimes the total and the number of bays are given and the child must set how many crates go in each bay; sometimes the total and crates-per-bay are given and he must set the number of bays; and at least two orders are impossible — the total cannot be divided evenly into the demanded bays (for example 26 crates into 4 bays, 45 crates into 6 bays). For those, the only correct action is slamming the REFUSE lever, and the dock ledger asks him to name the two totals nearby that WOULD have worked. Use unseen number families beyond 5×6 and 6×4 — go into 7s, 8s, 9s, and totals up to 90. When he sets a wrong bay count, the crates visibly load and one bay ends up short or overflowing, the barge horn blows, and the order sails with a hole in the manifest. Escalate: order five gives two constraints at once (a total, a minimum crates-per-bay, and a bay count he must choose that satisfies both); order six is the impossible one dressed to look easy. End with the manifest ledger read back to him — every order he shipped, every order he correctly refused, and every hole he left — then let him decide whether he takes tomorrow's shift.
input.nextStakesDesign: The manifest is what is at risk. Each order shipped with an uneven load punches a permanent hole in the night's manifest, and holes are shown in the end-of-shift ledger with the exact order that caused them. Three holes and the dispatcher pulls him off the dock mid-shift — the run ends early, the remaining orders sail without him, and he sees which ones he never got to touch. Refusing an order that was actually shippable also costs: that barge leaves empty and counts as a hole too, so 'refuse everything' is not a hiding place.
input.nextFailureMode: Two ways to lose. Forcing an impossible split — loading 26 crates into 4 bays and shipping it — leaves a visible short bay and a manifest hole. Refusing a shippable order leaves an empty barge and a manifest hole. Three holes ends the shift early with orders still on the conveyor he will never see. This can be failed, and it should be: the whole point is that a child who has been right nine times in a row learns nothing from an instrument that cannot tell him no.
input.nextEscalation: Orders one and two state the total and the bay count — he supplies group size only, conveyor slow. Order three flips the unknown to bay count without announcing it. Order four is the first impossible order, arriving at normal speed with no warning. Order five stacks two constraints so a single bay count must satisfy both a total and a minimum load. Order six is impossible but wears friendly round numbers, and by then the conveyor is fast enough that hesitating costs him the order.
input.nextMechanicSpec: The child's finger drags a stack of crates from the conveyor onto a numbered bay strip at the bottom of the screen, and pinches or taps a dial to set how many bays open. As he turns the dial the bays physically split apart on screen and the crate stack redistributes live, so an uneven setting shows one bay visibly taller or one bay half-empty before he commits. Committing is a tap on the barge horn. Refusing is a hard drag down on the red REFUSE lever at screen right, which flips the order off the conveyor and back up the ramp. Failure looks like this: the barge pulls away, the camera stays on the short bay with its gap of missing crates, a red hole stamps onto the manifest card in the corner, and the hole count ticks up. At three, the dispatcher's hand comes into frame, the conveyor belt stops, and the remaining order cards slide past greyed out.
input.nextMathematicalHook: Some numbers simply refuse to be shared out evenly, and you can prove it before you move a single crate — 26 will never fill 4 bays, no matter how you shuffle it, but 24 and 28 will. The whoa is discovering that 'this cannot be done' is a real mathematical answer, and that he can spot it faster than the machine can load it.
